title: Doubling Graph Traversal Efficiency to 198 TeraTEPS on the Supercomputer Fugaku
problem: Distributed breadth-first search (BFS) on large graphs is hindered by high communication costs when exchanging vertex data between compute nodes. Memory footprint constraints prevent smaller numbers of nodes from managing very large graphs efficiently.
motivation: BFS is a fundamental building block in HPC applications and a key Graph500 benchmark, making efficient distributed BFS essential for processing increasingly large datasets.
method: The paper introduces four complementary techniques: (i) forest pruning eliminates unnecessary vertices from the search space; (ii) group reordering decreases memory footprint; (iii) multilevel bitmap compression further reduces memory usage, enabling fewer nodes to manage larger graphs; and (iv) adaptive parameter tuning quickly optimizes BFS hyperparameters. These techniques jointly address communication bottlenecks and memory constraints.
key_novelty: Combining forest pruning with multilevel bitmap compression to simultaneously reduce both the active vertex search space and memory footprint, enabling efficient scaling to hundreds of thousands of nodes.
contributions: Forest pruning technique to eliminate unnecessary vertices during BFS traversal
Group reordering and multilevel bitmap compression for memory footprint reduction
Adaptive parameter tuning framework for BFS optimization
Achieved 198 TeraTEPS on Fugaku (152,064 nodes), doubling previous best results
